newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU presents more liberal telecoms offer at talks.
newsitem.headline: EU presents more liberal telecoms offer at talks.

text.p: The European Union presented a more liberal proposal at global telecommunications negotiations Wednesday as talks on a pact to ease controls on the $600 billion market moved ahead of a Saturday deadline.

EU chief negotiator Karl Falkenberg said the revised offer contained commitments on the liberalisation of all basic telecommunications sub-sectors and excluded broadcasting to the public from the definition of basic telecommunications services.
The revision also included technical improvements and took into account the views of fellow trading partners on frequencies and management policies for satellite and radio operators.
"We think we have reached a point where most if not all of our partners recognise that these distinctions are appropriate," Falkenberg told a news briefing.
Canadian trade officials also said they would consider further improvements in their proposal regarding domestic satellite communications and look into ways of opening them up to foreign operators.

Fifty-nine governments representing more than 90 percent of the global market have submitted offers to open their domestic telecommunications markets to foreign operators. Sri Lanka and Tanzania were expected to present offers by the end of the week.

"As of today, we have well over 90 percent of the world revenue in telecoms covered by offers of different participants," Falkenberg said. "We certainly think that this is an achievement that would make it impossible for members not to conclude the talks. This is substansive coverage."

U.S. negotiators are conducting an assessment of whether they have the "critical mass" of quality offers Washington says it needs to guarantee unfettered foreign access to is own market, the world's biggest.

U.S. negotiators were believed to be concentrating on wresting improvements from South Korea, Canada and Mexico, according to trade sources. To a lesser extent, Brazil and India were also being pressured to make further concessions.
The United States derailed an effort last April to reach a global pact when it backed away, saying offers from emerging economies were insufficient.
